title: The Conveyor Belt: Build your School Systems
author: Chris O’Brien
summary: Chris O'Brien, drawing on Chapter 1 of his book The Systemic Principal, argues that the prevailing hero principal model is wrong because it makes a school depend on one person's will. He opens with the seamless Carvana car purchase as an example of invisible architecture behind a smooth experience. He then recounts a chaotic enrollment process in a school network and the six-step method used to fix it: map it, sequence it, connect it, clarify it, minimize it, learn from it. The principal's real job, he says, is to design, implement and monitor systems that let every adult do their best work. The piece closes with diagnostic questions for redesigning any system a leader currently holds together by effort.
points: The principal's actual job is designing and monitoring the systems that let every adult in the building work well, not personally holding everything together.
A system is a designed sequence in which each step triggers the next, whereas many school routines are only accumulated activities running on inertia.
Handoffs that depend on someone remembering should be redesigned so the system, not a person, triggers them.
Without a designated owner, work defaults to the person with the most authority, so the leader must deliberately minimize their role everywhere except where only they can act.
Feedback loops only build trust if people visibly see changes made in response.
quotes: The principal’s actual job is designing, implementing, and monitoring the systems that allow every adult in the building to do their best work so every student can do theirs. Most leadership development programs never address that sentence.
A conveyor belt moves things through a predefined sequence with a specific function at each stage to arrive at a defined outcome. Nothing happens out of order. Nothing gets skipped.
Clear is kind. Vague is how a well-intentioned system becomes ten different systems running under the same name.

Cohesion determines whether a system runs on compliance or commitment. When everyone is operating from the same information, in the same sequence, with the same understanding of what the system is designed to produce, people can make good decisions independently.

The hero principal’s role in every system is enormous, not because they designed it that way, but because nobody else was designed to own it. When no one is designated, everything defaults to the person with the most authority and the strongest sense of responsibility.
A feedback mechanism that doesn’t visibly change anything is worse than no feedback mechanism. It teaches people their experience doesn’t matter.
